claims.text: Adding a minor self-lubricating dopant to CoCrFeNi will maintain low friction and wear from room temperature to 800 °C.
The starting CoCrFeNi alloy has a conventional single-phase, coarse to moderately refined grain structure.
Minor alloying with a self-lubricating element will induce an adaptive surface modification during sliding.
The dopant will promote grain-boundary and surface phase transformations.
The proposed transformations will produce an ultrafine nanocrystalline lubricious glaze layer.
The glaze layer will be enriched in the added dopant.
At lower temperatures, dopant-associated grain refinement will cause inverse Hall-Petch softening.
Inverse Hall-Petch softening will lower surface shear strength and friction.
At higher temperatures, the dopant will facilitate formation of a stable lubricious oxide or glaze layer.
A dense nanocrystalline glaze layer can minimize adhesive and oxidative wear at 800 °C.
Mixed metal-oxide surface films can reduce wear in high-entropy alloys.
The doped CoCrFeNi alloy will have a friction coefficient near 0.2 throughout the room-temperature-to-800 °C range.
The doped CoCrFeNi alloy will have wear rates of approximately 10^-7 to 10^-6 mm³/N·m throughout the room-temperature-to-800 °C range.
The doped alloy will exhibit lower friction and wear than undoped CoCrFeNi.
Undoped CoCrFeNi has higher friction and wear under variable conditions because of grain coarsening or unstable oxide-film formation.
The beneficial effect is expected only under sliding conditions that permit formation of the adaptive surface layer.
Very high oxygen pressure or unanticipated loading regimes may change phase formation and effectiveness.
The experiment will compare doped and undoped CoCrFeNi by ball-on-disk testing from room temperature to 800 °C while measuring friction, wear, and surface structure.
